KEY MESSAGE 1...A strengthening storm system organizes off the 
northern Mid-Atlantic coast today into Friday.

A vigorous upper-level trough continues to be forecast to 
evolve across the eastern U.S. from today into the weekend. 
This supports a surface low tracking over the Mid-Atlantic that  
will then transition its energy to a developing area of low 
pressure offshore which will tend to consolidate off the New 
Jersey coast later today, and deepen as it tracks north- 
northeast toward the Canadian Maritimes on Friday into Saturday.
While there are still some differences with the handling of the
embedded shortwaves, there is better model clustering with the 
surface low placement/track. Overall, it will be unsettled 
across our region as we go through today and Friday.

While showers have developed over northwestern portions of the 
area late tonight as the initial low tracks towards the area, 
the bulk of precipitation looks to hold off until the afternoon 
hours today. Any showers may be moderate to occasionally heavy 
at times, where even a few embedded thunderstorms cannot be 
ruled out. Guidance continues to indicate an uptick in the 
instability department, albeit is very meager at best around 
250-500 J/kg. Guidance has also hinted at a localized 
convergence zone as the low transitions some energy offshore. 
While strongest flow aloft is displaced to our south and west, 
bulk shear values will be around 40 kt. As a result, SPC has 
introduced a Marginal Risk for severe weather today (primarily 
in the afternoon hours). Primary threat would be localized 
damaging winds, but also cannot rule out a few instances of hail
with cold temperatures aloft. Overall, this set-up is low CAPE,
modest shear, so confidence in occurrence is less than usual.

The strength of the parent upper-level trough results in a 
colder air mass moving in with time, however the initial air 
mass is not all that cold (the lack of a cold antecedent air 
mass). As the surface low consolidates off the northern Mid-
Atlantic coast, the winds will turn more out of the northwest 
and this will increase the cold air advection. This will result 
in some colder air seeping southeastward later tonight but 
especially Friday into Friday night. The air mass may become 
sufficiently cold enough mostly across our far northwestern 
zones for some snow across the higher elevations, confined 
mainly to the Pocono Plateau. Any snowfall accumulation is 
expected to be less than an inch. Some elevated locations across
the Lehigh Valley and Northwestern NJ may see a few wet flakes 
mixing in, but no accumulations are expected. Otherwise, a rain 
event is forecast. The amount of precipitation (rain and/or 
snow) will depend on the ultimate track of the surface low and 
whether a deformation zones wraps back into our northern to 
central areas. At the moment, rainfall amounts north of the PA 
Turnpike to I-195 corridor range around the 0.50-1.25" range 
while further south across Philly and south, we are expecting 
less than 0.50" of rainfall, with less than 0.10" expected for 
the southern Delmarva. 

The model consensus looks to be more of a northward positioning
of the surface low, which if this ends up occurring would 
result in less rainfall with a southward extent across our area.
Consequently, the forecast rainfall have diminished a bit. The 
coastal impacts, including the potential for stronger onshore 
winds and also (minor) tidal flooding, are a little less certain
because the surface low track right over our area would lessen 
the residence time of the (stronger) onshore flow. Prior to the 
low fully consolidating offshore, some elevated instability 
could get into especially portions of our coastal plain and 
therefore a rumble of thunder is possible later tonight and 
Friday morning. The strongest winds with this look to occur as 
the storm moves farther away and the cold air advection then 
increases from the northwest. The main uncertainty is on how 
much precipitation occurs with this event region-wide and the 
extent/amount of any higher elevation snow (mainly for the 
southern Poconos). 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Minor tidal flooding expected with this 
morning's high tide.

A brief period of onshore flow will result in some elevated
tides. For the most part, tidal flooding will be relatively
spotty for communities along the Atlantic Ocean and Delaware
Bay. More widespread tidal flooding though is currently forecast
for areas around Barnegat Bay, which could result in some 
inundation of low lying areas and roadways this morning. As a 
result, a Coastal Flood Advisory was issued for Ocean County. 

No other headlines are in place. No tidal flooding is expected 
along the tidal Delaware River and Chesapeake Bay. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...A stretch of below normal temperatures begins 
on Friday, continuing through the weekend as a much colder 
airmass moves overhead.
